# Introduction
We are going to estimate a model using `xgboost`, a black-box method, for the Boston dataset. Then we try to make it explainable with a surrogate, including RuleFit (with `pre`). We will also compute variable importances with Shapley values using `fastshap` 

The motivation to provide RuleFit surrogates and interpretation with Shapley values for importance comes from [(Molnar, 2025)](#r2).

Here we use a `tidymodels` workflow for the estimation.  

# Packages
As usual, we have some standard packages. 
```{r}
library(ISLR2) #data
library(mbadtools) # some extra ggplot functions
conflicted::conflict_prefer_matching("select|filter", "dplyr", quiet=TRUE)
# interpretability
source("gg_interpret.R")
library(vip)
conflicted::conflicts_prefer(vip::vi, .quiet=TRUE) # the other vi() is a text editor
library(pdp)
library(pre)
# library(fastshap) # included in `vip`
```

# Data
We'll use the `Boston` dataset from the `ISLR2` package.
```{r}
data("Boston")
Boston %>% skim
```

There's no missing data, all 13 are numeric, and `chas` appears to be binary. the target variable will be `medv`, the median value of homes in a community.

# Workflow with `tidymodels` 
There are multiple steps. Set a seed for reproducibility.
```{r}
set.seed(2025)
```

# Data
We looked at the `Boston` dataset before.

# Crossvalidation split
Split the data into training and test datasets. We use an 80-20 split.
```{r}
set.seed(2025)
split <- initial_split(Boston, prop = 0.8, strata = medv)  # medv is the outcome
train_data <- training(split)
test_data  <- testing(split)
```

# Recipe
This is a basic approach. The recipe creates the formula and the data in a standard manner. It also allows some modification such as scaling and removing variables with little variance, that is almost constant and therefore unable to affect anything.

No fancy preprocessing, but center/scale numeric predictors. Most AI models work better with scaled predictors (drivers). Model `medv` using all other variables.
```{r}
boston_recipe <- recipe(medv ~ ., data = train_data) %>%
  step_nzv(all_predictors()) %>%  # remove near-zero variance if any
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) # center & scale numeric predictors
```

# Black-Box Model
We model with `xgboost`, a popular and quite good model. The modeling code is in the `parsnip` package.
```{r}
xg_spec <- boost_tree() %>%
  set_engine("xgboost") %>% 
  set_mode("regression")

xg_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_model(xg_spec) %>%
  add_recipe(boston_recipe)

# Fit linear model on training data
xg_fit <- xg_workflow %>% fit(data = train_data)
```

# Evaluate Metrics
```{r}
xg_pred <- predict(xg_fit, test_data) %>%
  bind_cols(test_data) %>%
  rename(.pred = .pred)
```

Compute metrics: 
The `metrics` function is from the `yardstick` package. Remember we selected the metrics to use earlier.
```{r}
xg_metrics <- xg_pred %>% metrics(truth = medv, estimate = .pred)
xg_metrics
```

The model achieved almost 89% r-squared and an rmse of 3.35 thousand dollars.

# Variable importance
For interpretation of 'black box' models we need to do something to explain the predictions. Read [(Molnar, 2025)]($r2) for more on interpretability calculations. One such is variable importance. 

We can extract the fitted values and variable importance from the random forest from `parsnip` using `vip`. For the linear model, the variable importance is defined as the absolute value of the coefficient of the variable. We will use `vip::vi` to construct the data when there is no `variable.importance` created by the `parsnip` model 

Extract `parsnip` fit object. Get a common data object to plot by using `vip::vi` for the model, and use model-agnostic permutation importances instead of those automatically done by the `xgboost` model.

We need to construct a prediction function for the `xgboost` result. This function works for a `tidymodels` workflow, a `parsnip` model, or a raw `xgboost` model.

```{r}
# Permutation-based variable importance

pred_wrapper <- function(object, newdata) {
  # If it's a workflow (parsnip + recipe)
  if (inherits(object, "workflow")) {
    # Make sure you pass a data.frame with all predictor columns
    predict(object, new_data = newdata) %>% 
      dplyr::pull(.pred)
  } 
  # If it's a parsnip model_fit
  else if (inherits(object, "model_fit")) {
    predict(object, new_data = newdata) %>% 
      dplyr::pull(.pred)
  } 
  # If it's a raw xgboost Booster
  else if (inherits(object, "xgb.Booster")) {
    predict(object, as.matrix(newdata)) %>% 
      dplyr::pull(.pred)
  } else {
    stop("Unsupported object type for pred_wrapper")
  }
}
```

Now we calculate permutation importances using `vip`. Randomization in the permutations requires setting a seed for reproducibility.
```{r}
set.seed(123)

xg_vi_perm <- vi(
  xg_fit,
  method = "permute",
  train = train_data,
  target = "medv",
  metric = "rmse",
  nsim = 5,
  pred_wrapper=pred_wrapper,
  smaller_is_better = TRUE
)

# View results
xg_vi_perm
```

We plot the vip.
<a name="Figure1"/>
```{r fig.width=12}
xg_vi_perm %>% gg_vip() + labs(subtitle="xgboost")
```


`lstat` and `rm` are the most important variables in the model. Remember that xgboost is based on random choices, so you could get different importances with another run. 

# Partial dependence 
Partial dependence plots show the marginal effect of a feature (or two) on the predicted outcomes. [(Molnar, n.d.)](#r2) 

Find the 2 top variables from the black-box model:
```{r}
top_var_xg <- xg_vi_perm$Variable[1:2]
cat("\nxgboost Top variables by importance: ", top_var_xg)
```

Partial dependence plots on the top two variables, using `pdp` to extract the proper data. Construct the data for plotting:
```{r}
# use pdp to get data to plot
xg_fit_obj <- extract_fit_parsnip(xg_fit)$fit

pd_xg1 <- pdp::partial(object=xg_fit, pred.var = "lstat", 
                   train = train_data,
                   pred.fun = pred_wrapper,
                   plot=FALSE)
 
pd_xg2 <- pdp::partial(xg_fit, pred.var = "rm", 
                   train = train_data,
                   pred.fun = pred_wrapper,
                   plot=FALSE)
```

Plot the constructed data frames.  Rug plots, to show the density of the axis variables, are a good idea, according to [(Molnar, Chapter 19)](#r2). 

I like the dot plots better. We put the plots side by side.
<a name="Figure2"/>
```{r}
wrap_plots(ncol=2,
      gg_pdp(pd_xg1),
      gg_pdp(pd_xg2)
      )
```
The relation is clearly not linear for the black-box model. The plot shows a steady decline till a break at an `lstat` of about 1 sd above the mean, when it flattens out.  That value of `lstat` is `r mean(Boston$lstat) + sd(Boston$lstat)`, or around 20%. For `rm` the plot is an S curve going up between 6.5 and 7.5 rooms.

# SHAP Importance
Shapley values are a different method of calculating importance.
```{r}
  vi_shap(xg_fit, train=train_data, 
          feature_names=colnames(xg_fit$pre$mold$predictors),
          pred_wrapper=pred_wrapper,
          nsim=30) %>%
    gg_vip(width=.7) + labs(subtitle = "chas==0")
```


```{r}
# library(fastshap) # `fastshap` is included in `vip` package
library(shapviz)
shap <- fastshap::explain(xg_fit, X = train_data %>% select(-medv), 
                          nsim = 10, 
                          pred_wrapper = pred_wrapper, 
                          shap_only=FALSE,
                )
X_pred = data.matrix(train_data %>% select(-medv, lstat, rm))
baseline= X_pred %>% mean()
sviz = shapviz(shap, 
               X_pred = X_pred,
               baseline = baseline)
```

<a name="Figure3"/>
```{r fig.height=10, fig.width=12}
wrap_plots(ncol=2,
           sviz %>% sv_importance(show_numbers=TRUE),
           sviz %>% sv_importance(kind="beeswarm")
)
```

Interpreting Shapley values is a whole story. You have to read [Molnar, 2025](#r1) on Shapley values. 

The mean ones on the left function kind of like variable importances. The individual ones in the right-hand plot show how the variable contributes to the individual observation predictions. You can see that `lstat` produces a big swing in `medv` from positive to negative, in line with its large importance.

Another often-used plot is a waterfall plot. This by default plots the effect on a single observation (the first one). You can select observations and then you get the mean effects.
```{r}
sviz %>% sv_waterfall()
sviz %>% sv_waterfall(row_id = c(1:nrow(train_data)))
```

Shapley importances may be harder to explain than the black-box model itself. I can say this with some confidence,since I wrote my dissertation on cooperative games including the Shapley value concept.

# Surrogate Model
We build a RuleFit type surrogate decision tree model using the `pre` package. See [Friedman and Popescu (2008)](#r3) for information on RuleFit surrogates.
```{r}
pre_model <- pre(medv ~ ., data = train_data, family = "gaussian", ntrees = 100)
```

Plot a summary of the prediction rule ensemble model. In tree construction randomness is used. WE plot only the first 9 terms and exclude linear effects.

<a name="Figure4"/>
```{r fig.height=10, fig.width=12}
plot(pre_model, nterms=9, linear.terms=FALSE)
```

Most important rules:
```{r}
pre::importance(pre_model, plot=F)$baseimps %>% head(6)
```
Retrieve the importances and make a vip graph.
```{r}
pre::importance(pre_model) #graph
```
Make predictions on `test_data`:
```{r}
xg_predictions <- predict(xg_fit, new_data = test_data) %>% 
  pull(.pred)
pre_predictions <- predict(pre_model, newdata = test_data)
```

Calculate r-squared and rmse for the `xgboost` model and the `pre` model.
```{r}
xg_rsq <- yardstick::rsq_vec(test_data$medv, xg_predictions)
pre_rsq <- yardstick::rsq_vec(test_data$medv, pre_predictions)
xg_rmse <- yardstick::rmse_vec(test_data$medv, xg_predictions)
pre_rmse <- yardstick::rmse_vec(test_data$medv, pre_predictions)

tibble( model = c("xgboost","pre"),
        rsq = c(xg_rsq, pre_rsq),
        rmse = c(xg_rmse, pre_rmse))
```

The pre surrogate explained about 87% of the variation in the black-box model predictions.

# Conclusion
We used `tidymodels` to model the `Boston` dataset predicting `medv` from the other variables. We tried an `xgboost` black-box model with default tuning.

On the way we found the importance of variables in the `xgboost`, with `lstat`and `rm` being most important. We made variable importance plots side by side. [Figure 1](#Figure1) shows the comparison of Variable Importance for the two models. [Figure 2](#Figure2) shows partial dependence plots for `lstat` and `rm`. 

We also produced Shapley value importances, both mean and individual. While they are more complicated to explain than the black-box model itself, they have the advantage of guaranteeing fairness of spreading the contributions of the variables. They are shown in [Figure 3](#Figure3)

Finally we prepared a surrogate model with `pre` in the form of a small decision tree. It is kind of easy to explain and captures about 86% of what the black-box predicted. We can see the decision tree in [Figure4](#Figure4)
